problem_setting.description: The paper addresses a measurement problem in modern large language model inference: commonly reported GPU utilization does not directly reveal whether expensive execution resources are doing useful work. The authors focus on NVIDIA Hopper-class GPUs and ask which architectural resources actually limit decode and prefill execution across representative serving workloads. They distinguish nominal device activity from effective utilization of tensor cores, scalar and vector execution pipelines, memory bandwidth, cache capacity, and interconnect resources. This distinction matters because a kernel can keep the GPU busy while still leaving the performance-critical execution units substantially underused, so aggregate utilization can mislead optimization and capacity-planning decisions.

method_components.name: Hierarchical profiling
method_components.description: The study combines end-to-end workload profiling with kernel-level hardware-counter analysis. Instead of treating GPU utilization as a single scalar, it decomposes execution into attention, matrix multiplication, communication, normalization, sampling, and other kernels, then inspects achieved throughput, occupancy, memory traffic, cache behavior, and execution-pipeline activity. This hierarchy lets the authors connect application-level latency and throughput to concrete microarchitectural bottlenecks and identify cases where a busy GPU is not effectively using the resources that determine performance.

method_components.name: Resource-centric utilization model
method_components.description: The analysis organizes measurements around the Hopper resources that can independently become limiting factors, including tensor-core compute, CUDA-core pipelines, high-bandwidth memory, on-chip caches, and communication links. For each workload phase and kernel family, the authors compare achieved rates against the relevant architectural ceilings rather than relying on a generic utilization percentage. This resource-centric view exposes whether a workload is compute-bound, bandwidth-bound, latency-bound, synchronization-bound, or limited by insufficient parallelism, and it highlights bottlenecks hidden by conventional monitoring metrics.

method_components.name: Cross-workload characterization
method_components.description: The paper evaluates multiple inference configurations that vary model structure, sequence length, batch size, and execution phase so that conclusions are not tied to a single serving point. Prefill and decode are examined separately because they stress different parts of the GPU, while representative kernels are compared across workload shapes. By correlating these workload dimensions with low-level counters, the study identifies recurring utilization patterns and explains why optimization opportunities shift as batching, token position, attention shape, and communication requirements change.

method_components.name: Optimization diagnosis
method_components.description: The authors use the measured resource gaps to reason about optimization priorities rather than assuming that higher occupancy or higher reported GPU utilization automatically improves inference. They identify when additional fusion, batching, memory-traffic reduction, communication overlap, or kernel specialization is likely to matter and when it is unlikely to address the actual bottleneck. The resulting methodology is intended as a diagnostic framework for inference-system designers: first identify the underused critical resource, then choose an optimization that targets that resource and validate the change with the same low-level measurements.
